entries.english: The 13 Historical Giriama Circumcision Cycles (Marika, Taylor 1891 pp. 2, 21)
entries.translation: (1) Wula-mbere ('First-rains'), (2) Wula-kahi ('Middle-rains'), (3) Wula-nyuma ('Latter-rains'), (4) T'ungudza ('Tomatoes'), (5) P'uku ('Large wild rats'), (6) Nguluwe ('Pigs'), (7) Vitambi ('Coloured cloths'), (8) Vitsoka ('Hatchets'), (9) Abi-Kizi ('Kizi's-father'), (10) Atsai ('Wizards'), (11) Mafira ('Puff-adders'), (12) Mitseka ('Mats'), (13) Nyoga ('Feathers' — current cycle in 1891, with 'Kavuta' as its 1st sub-rika)
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'Giryama Vocabulary and Collections', p. 2 under Age & p. 21 under Circumcision-cycles

entries.english: Giriama Elder Governance & Initiation Lodge Degrees (Habasi & K'ambi, Taylor 1891 pp. 37–38, 79)
entries.translation: Preliminaries: Uhoho → Umondo → Ubora | 1st Degree Habasi (Ahoho a Habasi-ni / Nyere under hierophant Muhagizi → Ahoho a Mihaso-ni) | 4 Dances to 2nd Degree K'ambi: (1) Gawe (with Mwandza M'kulu mystic drum under M'kuzi), (2) Sayo ra K'oma (under Mwenye Sayo), (3) M'ng'aro, (4) Kirao (with musichana bamboo drum; wearing luwoo armlet at Nyambura feast & sitting in M'oro parliament) | Senior Elders (Azhere): Waya (bandari club-house) & Fisi ('Hyena' inner circle under M'kuzi, then Mwa-Rima) → 3 Enye-ts'i ('Possessors of the Land')
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'Giryama Vocabulary and Collections', pp. 37–38 under Freemasonry & p. 79 under Orders

entries.english: The 30-Day Giriama Month (3 Makumi), 4-Day Market/Farming Week & Seasons (Taylor 1891 pp. 56, 103, 134)
entries.translation: 3 Decades (Makumi): kumi ra kwandza, kumi ra kahi, kumi ra kuzimu (new moon hailed with 'Ko——ngo!') | 4-Day Week: (1) Jumwa, (2) Kuramuka, (3) Kurima-hiri, (4) Kuisa | 6-Day Future Sequence (p. 103): rero, machero, muhondo, gorya, mweriyao, mweriyao wa tuto | Seasons (p. 134): Mwaka (March/April Great Rains), Mwaka Musha (Ingathering), Mutsuwo (July/August Lesser Rains), Vuri (October Latter Rains, 1st month Kutsano)

entries.english: The 12 Traditional Wanika (Mijikenda) Agricultural Months Across Masika, Furi & Kaskazi (Krapf 1882, p. 205 under masíka)
entries.translation: Masika & Furi (April–Nov, 8 farming months): (1) Muezi wa muanzo wa muaka (April — sowing mahindi), (2) Muezi wa viri (May), (3) Muezi wa tahu (June — maize ripens), (4) Muezi wa nne (July — first harvest; furi begins), (5) Muezi wa tzano (Aug — second sowing of maize), (6) Muezi wa handáhu (Sept), (7) Muezi wa fungáhu (Oct), (8) Muezi wa nane (Nov — second harvest) • Madjira ya kaskázi (Dec–March, 4 festival/dry months): (9) Muézi wa matzúla (Dec — tapping coconut palms), (10) Kurri bómu / kurri wa muanzo (Jan — great festival, no field work), (11) Kurri ya magáro (Feb — youth age-grade festival), (12) Muezi wa bózo / Muisho wa kaskazi (March — playing the záyo fiddle before clearing plantations)

Mudzalamuka? — Hudzalamuka. — Na hulamuke! | Aged Midday: Tsanani! — Hmwishamwe! Mudzadherwa? — Hudzadherwa. — Na hudherwe! | Aged Evening: Dziloni! — Hmwishamwe! Kwatswa? — Kudzatswa! | Parting: Kala uworo! — Haya, enda matsiya!

entries.translation: Ancient Rabai capitals on Mount Reale: Mutzi Muíru (Mutzi mubomu wa Reale) & Mutzi Mudide (later called Mitzi ya Ntzoáni, led by fierce elders Gníro & Nchira); Malando & Kamfuda clans dispersed to Rombo in Chagga, Wadigo, and the Pokomo river, while one division sought refuge with their brother-tribe Chogni (Chogni cha Muadarúko), founded Kaya Vokéra for 9 generations, and later founded Mutzi Múvia (Rabbai M'pia) • Two Brother-Tribe Confederacies: (I) Muravai, Muchogni, Mukiriama, Mtahe; (II) Duruma, Rive, Kambe, Káuma • War-Council at Tziwe ra kizungu & Kizúmo / Salala Chant against Rabai Maboma: 'hukutáne, huenende, hukafunse mutzi hio wa Aravai' → 'Muravai! kuna ndugu! entries.english: Dr. Krapf's (1850, p. vi) Wanika Ethnography, Mulungu Cosmology & Origin Traditions (Jagga, Ambakómo, Mángea)
entries.translation: Wanika Population & Polity (p. vi): ~50,000–60,000 souls living in woodland villages at 1,200–2,000 ft elevation, 15–20 miles inland between 3° and 5° S, governed by a republican council of elders (azee / kambi), believing in a Supreme Being called Mulungu ("heaven") and offering sacrifices at ancestral graves (koma) • Four Historical Migration Traditions (p. vi): (1) Rabbai (Rabai) claim their ancestors emigrated from Jagga (Kilimanjaro), where a related tribe still bears their name; (2) Wateita of Kadiáro, Ndara, and Bura call the Wanika "Ambakómo" because part of the Wanika formerly lived in the country of Pokómo (Tana River) before fleeing the Galla; (3) Wasegéju near Tanga likewise claim descent from Wapokómo expelled by the Galla; (4) Kiriama (Giriama) assert their forefathers lived at Mount Mángea near the Pokomóni
